column2: Partners A and B share 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5, taken equally from A and B. Their new shares are 1/2, 3/10 and 1/5, and A:B sacrificing ratio is 1:1.
column3: In that admission, A:B sacrificing ratio remains 3:2 because that was their old profit-sharing ratio.

column2: A:B:C share 1/2:3/10:1/5. B retires and A:C become 3:2. Their gains are 1/10 and 1/5, giving A:C gaining ratio 1:2.
column3: In that retirement, A:C gaining ratio is 3:2 because goodwill compensation follows only the final profit-sharing ratio.

column2: Average profit Rs 1,20,000, capital employed Rs 8,00,000 and normal return 10% give super profit Rs 40,000; three years' purchase gives goodwill Rs 1,20,000.
column3: Those figures give super profit Rs 1,20,000 because normal return is applied only after valuing goodwill.

column2: A pre-admission revaluation gain allocated to old partners in their old ratio compensates for value accrued before admission; using the new ratio would give the incoming partner part of that pre-admission gain.
column3: A pre-admission revaluation gain should be allocated in the new ratio because the new partner participates in every historical gain once admitted.

column2: In the ordinary partnership dissolution settlement, third-party debts precede partner advances, and partner advances precede return of capital, subject to the governing legal arrangement.
column3: Ordinary dissolution settlement repays partner capital before third-party debts because partners bear the ultimate business risk.

column2: Forfeited Rs 10 fully called shares on which Rs 6 per share was received may be reissued as fully paid at Rs 7; the Rs 3 discount is covered by the Rs 6 forfeiture attributable to those shares.
column3: Those shares cannot be reissued at Rs 7 because every reissue discount must be restricted to the original securities premium alone.

column2: If only part of a forfeited lot is reissued, capital reserve is computed from forfeiture attributable to the reissued shares less their reissue discount; the unreissued portion remains in share forfeiture.
column3: Partial reissue transfers the entire lot's forfeiture balance to capital reserve immediately, including the amount attributable to unreissued shares.

column2: A receivable and matching payable between parent and subsidiary are eliminated in consolidation without extinguishing the separate legal entities' underlying claims.
column3: Eliminating the intragroup receivable in consolidated accounts legally cancels the payable in the subsidiary's separate books.

column2: Under the stated consolidation model, parent sales to a subsidiary generate Rs 20,000 profit still in closing inventory. Consolidated inventory and group profit are reduced by Rs 20,000.
column3: The downstream unrealised profit remains in consolidated inventory because the subsidiary paid the invoiced price in a legally valid sale.

column2: In an 80%-owned subsidiary, an upstream inventory profit Rs 10,000 eliminated from the subsidiary's post-acquisition profit reduces non-controlling interest's profit share by Rs 2,000 under the stated model.
column3: Eliminating that upstream profit leaves non-controlling interest's profit share unchanged because every elimination is charged wholly to the parent.

column2: Under a conventional acquisition-date consolidation analysis, subsidiary profits accumulated before acquisition affect the acquired net-assets analysis rather than becoming the parent's post-acquisition revenue profit.
column3: All subsidiary retained earnings at reporting date are the parent's post-acquisition profit regardless of when they arose.

column2: A capital reduction used to eliminate accumulated losses can change the capital structure without itself creating a cash inflow or operating profit.
column3: Writing off accumulated losses through capital reduction creates a matching operating cash receipt.

column2: Starting with profit before tax under the stated indirect method, depreciation is added back; an increase in trade receivables is deducted, other things equal.
column3: Depreciation is deducted and an increase in receivables is added because both items increase accounting profit.

column2: Acquiring an asset by issuing shares directly is a noncash investing-financing transaction, distinct from cash paid for an asset and cash received from a share issue.
column3: Direct acquisition by issuing shares must be shown as equal cash investing outflow and financing inflow although no cash changed hands.

column2: Current assets Rs 200 and current liabilities Rs 100 give ratio 2. Paying Rs 50 of those liabilities in cash raises the ratio to 3 while reducing cash liquidity in absolute rupees.
column3: That payment necessarily reduces the current ratio because cash decreases by Rs 50.

column2: A higher current ratio need not mean faster cash availability when its increase comes from slow-moving inventory and overdue receivables.
column3: A higher current ratio alone establishes a faster cash-conversion cycle irrespective of inventory and receivable quality.

column2: A purchase of a fixed asset for cash reduces working capital and cash, while collection of a current receivable changes cash without changing total working capital on the stated facts.
column3: Collection of a current receivable necessarily increases working capital by the cash collected.

column2: After split-off, joint costs already incurred are sunk for a further-processing decision; incremental revenue must be compared with incremental processing costs.
column3: The product with the largest allocated joint cost must be processed further even when incremental revenue is below incremental processing cost.

column2: With contribution Rs 30 using 3 machine hours for A and Rs 24 using 1 hour for B, B ranks first at a binding machine-hour constraint, subject to demand limits.
column3: A ranks first under that constraint because contribution per unit Rs 30 exceeds B's Rs 24.

column2: Buying at Rs 75 rather than making with variable cost Rs 60 and unavoidable allocated fixed cost Rs 25 is unfavourable if there is no alternative use or other relevant difference.
column3: Buying is favourable on those facts because the full allocated make cost Rs 85 exceeds Rs 75.

column1: Opportunity cost of idle versus constrained capacity
column2: A special order at Rs 70 with variable cost Rs 50 is assessed differently when capacity is idle than when fulfilling it displaces regular contribution Rs 30 per unit.
column3: The Rs 20 contribution makes the special order acceptable under both conditions because displaced contribution is not a cash expense.

column2: For standard quantity 100 kg at Rs 5 and actual quantity 110 kg at Rs 4, using purchased quantity equal to used quantity, price variance is Rs 110 favourable and usage variance Rs 50 adverse.
column3: Those figures give price variance Rs 100 favourable and usage variance Rs 40 adverse when the stated standard-cost method is used.

column2: Standard hours 80 at Rs 10 and actual hours 100 at Rs 9 give rate variance Rs 100 favourable and efficiency variance Rs 200 adverse under the stated standard-hours method.
column3: The favourable rate variance means total labour cost is favourable even though actual cost Rs 900 exceeds standard cost Rs 800.

column2: Comparing actual costs at 12,000 units with a budget flexed to 12,000 separates volume effects better than comparing them directly with the original 10,000-unit budget.
column3: A 10,000-unit fixed budget is the correct activity-adjusted benchmark for 12,000 actual units because flexing would conceal efficiency variances.

column2: In a process without losses, 800 completed units plus 200 closing units fully complete for materials and 40% complete for conversion yield 1,000 material and 880 conversion equivalent units under weighted average.
column3: That process yields 880 equivalent units for both materials and conversion because all inputs use the conversion completion percentage.

column2: Normal loss is anticipated in the process cost structure, whereas abnormal loss is separately identified rather than simply spreading every excess loss over good output as normal.
column3: Any excess loss above the specified normal rate is automatically absorbed as normal loss because both losses occur in the same process.

column2: An activity pool Rs 1,20,000 with 60 setups gives Rs 2,000 per setup; a product using 5 setups receives Rs 10,000 of that pool regardless of its direct labour hours.
column3: The product's setup charge is determined by direct labour hours even when setups are the specified cost driver.

column2: Market price Rs 500 and desired profit 20% of sales give target cost Rs 400; life-cycle analysis can include design and after-sales costs beyond factory production.
column3: Those figures give target cost Rs 416.67 because a sales-margin target is calculated as a markup on cost.

column2: Sufficient appropriate evidence concerns both quantity and quality; an unmodified opinion provides reasonable rather than absolute assurance and does not guarantee absence of every fraud.
column3: An unmodified opinion constitutes absolute assurance that no fraud has occurred because the auditor obtained sufficient evidence.

column2: Tracing a recorded purchase to supporting invoices tests a different assertion from physically inspecting inventory and assessing its valuation at period end.
column3: An invoice alone establishes existence, ownership and recoverable value of all closing inventory without additional verification.
